en: [Preface]
My dear children,

Some of you have already heard of the ancient Greeks. As you grow up, you will hear much more about them. The boys among you might spend a great deal of time reading Greek books. The girls may not learn the Greek language, but you will certainly come across many stories from Greek history. In fact, you will see things every day that we wouldn't have without these ancient Greeks. You can hardly find a well-written book that doesn't include Greek names, words, or proverbs. You can't walk through a large city without passing buildings designed in the Greek style. You can't enter a well-furnished room without seeing Greek statues, ornaments, or even furniture patterns. These ancient people have left a remarkable, lasting mark on our modern world. As you grow and read more, you'll discover just how much we owe them. They laid the foundation for our mathematics and geometry—the study of numbers, shapes, and the forces that move objects. They started our sciences of geography and astronomy. They also shaped our ideas of law, freedom, and politics, which teach us how to govern a peaceful and strong country. We even owe them our logic, the study of reasoning and words, and our metaphysics, the study of our own thoughts and souls. Finally, they made their language so beautiful that foreigners often preferred it to their own. Greek eventually became the common language of educated people across the ancient world, stretching from Persia and Egypt all the way to Spain and Britain. Because of this, the New Testament was written in Greek so that people across the entire Roman Empire could read and understand it. Aside from the Jewish people and the Bible they passed down to us, we owe more to the ancient Greeks than to anyone else on earth.

You must remember one important thing: 'Greeks' was not their real name. They always called themselves 'Hellens.' The Romans misnamed them Greeks, and we adopted that incorrect name from the Romans. It would take a long time to explain exactly why. The Hellens were made up of many different tribes and small, independent states. When you read in this book about the Minuai, the Athenians, and others, remember that they were all part of the one great Hellen race. They lived in the area we now call Greece, scattered across the islands of the Aegean Sea, and along the coast of Asia Minor (which they called Ionia), from the Hellespont to the island of Rhodes. Later, they built colonies and cities in Sicily and Southern Italy, a region known as Great Greece. They even settled along the shores of the Black Sea at places like Sinope, Kerch, and Sevastopol. Centuries later, they spread under the rule of Alexander the Great, conquering Egypt, Syria, Persia, and the entire East. But all of that happened hundreds of years after my stories take place. In the time of these tales, there were no Greeks on the Black Sea shores, in Sicily, in Italy, or anywhere outside of Greece and Ionia. If you ever feel puzzled by the place names in this book, pull out a map and track them down. It will be a much more pleasant way to learn geography than staring at a dull textbook.

I love these ancient Hellens deeply. I would be very ungrateful if I didn't, considering everything they have taught me. They feel like brothers to me, even though they died hundreds of years ago. Since you have to learn about them anyway, I want to be the first to introduce you. I say to you, "Come here, children, at this wonderful Christmas time. It is a season when all of God’s creatures should rejoice together and bless Him who saved us all. Come and meet my old friends. I knew them long before you were born. They have come to visit us at Christmas from the eternal world. They want to tell you some of the fairy tales they loved when they were young like you."

Nations begin as children, just like you, even though they are made up of grown adults. At first, they are men and women with the hearts of children. They are open, affectionate, trusting, and eager to learn about all the wonders around them. Too often, they are also greedy, passionate, and silly, exactly as children can be.

These ancient Greeks were eager to learn from all the nations around them. From the Phoenicians, they learned shipbuilding and perhaps the alphabet. From the Assyrians, they learned painting, carving, and how to build with wood and stone. From the Egyptians, they learned astronomy and many other complex subjects. In this way, they were like our own ancestors, the Northmen. You love hearing about them. Although the Northmen were wild and rough, they were humble and happy to learn from anyone. Because the Greeks were open-hearted and willing to be taught, God rewarded them just as He rewarded our ancestors. He made them wiser than the very people who taught them. God loves to see men and children eager to learn. He always gives more to those who use what they already have. So the Greeks grew wise and powerful. They wrote poems that will last until the end of the world—poems you must read for yourselves one day, at least in English, if not in Greek. They learned to carve statues and build temples that are still considered wonders of the world. God taught them many other wondrous things, and we are still benefiting from that wisdom today.
You must not think, children, that just because these ancient Greeks were pagans, God did not care for them or teach them anything.

The Bible tells us otherwise. It says that God's mercy covers all His creations, and that He understands the hearts of all people and shapes their work. Later, when the Greeks had grown wicked and fallen into decline, St. Paul told them they should have known better. After all, they were God's own children, just as their own poets had written. The good God had placed them where they were so they could seek the Lord and find Him, for He was never far from any of them. Clement of Alexandria, a wise and good Father of the early Church, even said that God sent philosophy down from heaven to the Greeks, just as He sent the Gospel down to the Jewish people.

Remember that Jesus Christ is the Light who guides everyone who comes into the world. No one can think a good thought, feel the right feeling, or understand the true nature of anything on earth or in heaven unless the good Lord Jesus teaches them through His Spirit.

However, as St. Paul reminded them, these Greeks eventually forgot what God had taught them. Even though they were God's children, they worshipped idols made of wood and stone. They fell into sin, shame, cowardice, and slavery. Ultimately, they were driven out of the beautiful land God had given them for so many years.

Like all great nations that leave behind more than just mounds of dirt, the Greeks initially believed in the One True God who created heaven and earth. But over time, like other nations, they began to worship other gods. These were actually angels and spirits who they believed lived across their land. They worshipped Zeus, the Father of gods and men, who was a faint memory of the true God. They also worshipped Hera, his wife; Apollo, the Sun-god; Athena, the goddess of wisdom and useful arts; Aphrodite, the Queen of Beauty; Poseidon, the Ruler of the Sea; and Hephaestus, the King of Fire, who taught men how to work with metals. They honored the gods of the rivers and the Nymphs, the nature spirits they imagined living in caves, fountains, forest glens, and beautiful wild places. They also feared the Furies, dreadful sisters who they believed haunted guilty men until their sins were forgiven. The Greeks had many other dreams that split the One God into many different figures. They even claimed these gods did terrible things that would be considered sinful for any human to do. When their own philosophers rose up and told them that God was One, they refused to listen. They loved their idols and wicked feasts until it brought them to ruin. But we will not talk about such sad things anymore.

At the time this little book takes place, they had not fallen that low. As far as I can tell, they did not worship idols. They still followed the moral rules of the last six commandments and knew right from wrong. They drew their courage from the belief that the gods loved men and taught them. They believed that without the gods, humanity would surely face ruin. In that respect, they were absolutely right—more right than they even realized. Without God, we can do nothing, because all wisdom comes directly from Him.

You must not picture the people in this book as the highly educated men who lived in the great cities of later times, creating beautiful works of art. Instead, imagine them as country people living a simple, hardworking life in farms and walled villages. The greatest kings and heroes cooked their own meals and felt no shame in it. They built their own ships, forged their own weapons, and fed and harnessed their own horses. The queens worked right alongside their maidservants. They managed the household, spun yarn, wove fabric, embroidered, and made clothes for themselves and their husbands. A man was honored not because he happened to be rich, but because of his skill, strength, courage, and the sheer number of things he could do. They were essentially grown-up children, but very noble ones. Just like at school today, the strongest and cleverest boy led the rest, even if he was poor.

While they were a young and simple civilization, they loved fairy tales just as much as you do now. All nations do when they are young. Our own ancestors told stories they called 'Sagas.' I will read you some of those one day—tales from the Eddas, the Voluspá, Beowulf, and the noble old romances. The ancient Arabs had their tales, which we now call the 'Arabian Nights.' The ancient Romans had theirs, called 'Fabulæ,' which gives us our word 'fable.' But the ancient Hellens called their stories 'Muthoi,' which is where we get the modern word 'myth.' Next to the old romances written during the Christian Middle Ages, there are no fairy tales quite like these ancient Greek ones. They are unmatched in beauty, wisdom, and truth. They inspire children to love noble deeds and to trust that God will help them through.

Why have I called this book 'The Heroes'? Because that was the name the Hellens gave to men who were brave, skilled, and dared to do more than others. At first, I think that was all the word meant. But over time, it came to mean something more. It came to mean men who helped their country. In those ancient times, when the land was half-wild, these men killed fierce beasts and evil criminals, drained swamps, and founded towns. After they died, they were honored because they left their country better than they found it. We still call such a person a hero in English today. We call it a 'heroic' act to suffer pain and grief just to do good for our fellow human beings. We can all do that, my children, boys and girls alike. We ought to do it, because it is easier and safer now than ever before, and the path is much clearer. But you are going to hear how the Hellens believed their heroes worked three thousand years ago. Of course, the stories are not entirely true—not even half of them. You are smart enough to know that. But the meaning behind them is true forever: do what is right, and God will help you.
Farley Court, Advent, 1855.
[Part 1: How Perseus and His Mother Came to Seriphos]

Once upon a time, there were twin princes named Acrisius and Proetus. They lived in the pleasant valley of Argos, far away in ancient Greece. They had fertile meadows, rich vineyards, sheep, oxen, and great herds of horses grazing down in the Lerna Fen. They had everything a man could need to be happy, yet they were miserable because they were intensely jealous of each other. They began to quarrel from the moment they were born. When they grew up, each tried to steal the other's share of the kingdom to keep it all for himself. First, Acrisius drove Proetus out. Proetus fled across the sea and returned with a foreign princess for a wife and an army of massive foreign builders known as Cyclopes. Proetus then drove Acrisius out. The two fought back and forth across the land for a long time until they finally settled the quarrel. Acrisius took the city of Argos and half the land, while Proetus took the city of Tiryns and the other half. Proetus and his giant Cyclopes built massive walls of rough, uncarved stone around Tiryns, which are still standing to this day.

One day, a prophet came to the hard-hearted King Acrisius and delivered a dark warning. "Because you have risen up against your own blood, your own blood shall rise up against you," the prophet said. "Because you have sinned against your family, your family will punish you. Your daughter, Danae, will bear a son, and you will die by that boy's hands. The gods have ordained it, and it will surely come to pass."

Acrisius was terrified, but he did not change his ways. He had always been cruel to his family, and instead of repenting and showing kindness, he became even more vicious. He locked his beautiful daughter, Danae, in an underground cavern lined with solid bronze so that no one could ever come near her. He thought he was outsmarting the gods, but you will soon see if anyone can truly escape them.

In time, Danae gave birth to a son. The baby was so beautiful that anyone but King Acrisius would have felt pity for him. But the king had no mercy. He dragged Danae and her infant down to the seashore, locked them inside a massive wooden chest, and shoved them out to sea. He left them for the winds and waves to carry wherever they pleased.

A brisk northwest wind blew out of the blue mountains, sweeping down the pleasant valley of Argos and out across the water. The mother and her baby floated away over the open sea. Everyone who watched them go wept for them, except for that cruel father, King Acrisius.

They floated on and on. The chest danced up and down upon the rolling waves, and the baby slept peacefully against his mother's breast. But the poor mother could not sleep. She stayed awake, watching the water and weeping. As they drifted, she sang a lullaby to her baby—a song you might learn yourselves one day.

Soon they drifted past the last blue headland and out into the open sea. There was nothing around them but waves, sky, and wind. Thankfully, the waves were gentle, the sky was clear, and the breeze was soft. These were the calm halcyon days of summer, a time when no storms ever ruffle the pleasant waters of the sea.
[Illustration: Danae and her baby adrift in the chest]

Who were Halcyone and Ceyx? You shall hear their story while the chest floats on. Halcyone was a fairy maiden, a daughter of the beach and the wind. She fell in love with a young sailor named Ceyx, and they were married. No one on earth was as happy as they were. But one day, Ceyx was shipwrecked. Before he could swim to shore, the massive waves swallowed him. Halcyone saw him drowning and leaped into the sea to save him, but it was too late. The gods took pity on the tragic lovers and transformed them into two beautiful sea-birds. Now, they build a floating nest every year and sail happily together forever upon the calm summer seas of Greece.

A night passed, and then a long, exhausting day for Danae. Another night and day went by. Danae grew weak and faint from hunger and weeping, yet there was still no land in sight. The baby slept quietly through it all. Finally, poor Danae let her head droop and fell asleep with her cheek resting against her child's.

A sudden, jarring grind woke her. The air was filled with a roaring sound. She looked up and saw massive cliffs towering over her, glowing red in the setting sun. Around her, the water crashed against jagged rocks, sending flakes of white foam flying through the air. She clasped her hands together and screamed for help. As she cried out, help arrived. A tall, stately man climbed over the rocks and looked down in wonder at poor Danae tossing in the chest among the waves.

He wore a rough woolen cloak and a broad hat to shade his face. He carried a heavy, three-pronged trident for spearing fish in one hand, and a casting net hung over his shoulder. Two servants followed him, carrying baskets for his catch. But Danae could tell from his impressive height, his confident walk, and his flowing golden hair and beard that he was no ordinary man. Before she could even get a good look at him, he dropped his trident, leaped down the rocks, and threw his heavy net perfectly over Danae and the chest. With a mighty pull, he dragged the chest, the mother, and the baby to safety onto a flat ledge of rock.
The fisherman gently took Danae by the hand, helped her out of the chest, and said,

"Beautiful lady, what strange accident has brought you to this island in such a fragile ship? Who are you, and where did you come from? Surely you must be a king's daughter. And this boy seems more than just mortal."
As he spoke, he pointed to the baby, whose face shone as brightly as the morning star.
Danae simply bowed her head and sobbed,
"Please, tell me what land I have reached, and what kind of men I have found here!"
"This island is called Seriphos," he replied. "I am a Greek, and I live here. I am the brother of King Polydectes. People call me Dictys the Netter, because I catch fish along the shore."
Danae fell to her knees at his feet and cried,

"Oh, sir, please have pity on a stranger driven to your land by a cruel fate! Let me live in your house as a servant, but treat me with honor. I was once a king's daughter, and this boy, as you guessed, comes from a noble bloodline. I will not be a burden to you or eat your food without earning it. I am more skilled at weaving and embroidery than any maiden in my homeland."
She would have continued, but Dictys gently stopped her. He raised her to her feet and said,

"My daughter, I am old and my hair is gray. I have no children of my own to bring joy to my home. Come with me. You shall be a daughter to me and my wife, and this baby will be our grandson. I fear the gods and always offer hospitality to strangers. I know that good deeds, just like evil ones, always return to the people who do them."
Danae was deeply comforted. She went home with Dictys, the good fisherman, and lived happily as a daughter to him and his wife for fifteen long years.
